note.explanation: A cell has structures that each perform particular jobs. Some provide support or control what enters and leaves; others store materials, make proteins, or help the cell move. Knowing each structure’s location and function helps you explain how a cell works.
examples: The cell wall gives plant cells strength and support.
The nucleus contains DNA and directs cell activities.
note.checkAnswer: Plasmodesmata are channels in cell walls that allow molecules to pass between adjacent cells.
note.simple: Think of a cell as a tiny working unit. Its parts have different jobs, like protecting it, controlling it, or moving materials.
note.checkQuestion: What are the channels in plant cell walls that allow molecules to pass between adjacent cells called?
note.title: Cell structures and their functions
steps: Identify the cell structure named in the question.
Recall its key feature or location.
State its function clearly, using the textbook’s terms.
note.answer: Cell structures have different features and functions. For example, the cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell, while the nucleus directs cellular activities.

mcqs.stem: Which layer holds together the primary walls of adjacent plant cells?
rationales: Correct: the middle lamella holds together the primary walls of adjacent cells.
The primary wall is a cellulose-rich wall layer, but it is not the layer joining adjacent cells.
The secondary wall may be made on the inner side of a primary wall in some plant cells.
The cell membrane surrounds the cytoplasm; it does not hold adjacent primary walls together.

mcqs.stem: What is the cell wall of fungi made of?
rationales: Peptidoglycan makes up the cell wall of prokaryotes.
Correct: fungal cell walls are made of chitin.
Cellulose is found in plant cell walls and the cell walls of algae.
Tubulin is a protein that makes up microtubules.

mcqs.stem: Which structure forms a double-membrane boundary around the nucleus?
rationales: Nucleoplasm is the jelly-like material inside the nucleus.
The nucleolus is a small body inside the nucleus where ribosomes are assembled.
Correct: the nuclear envelope is the double membrane around the nucleus.
Chromatin is thread-like material made of DNA and proteins inside the nucleus.

options: The nucleus moves to the centre
The nuclear envelope becomes the cell wall
mcqs.stem: What happens to chromatin when a cell starts dividing?
rationales: In mature plant cells, a large central vacuole can push the nucleus to the side; this is not what happens to chromatin during cell division.
Correct: chromatin condenses and takes the shape of thick chromosomes.
The nucleolus is where ribosomes are assembled; it does not become a vacuole.
The nuclear envelope does not become the cell wall.

mcqs.stem: What is the membrane of a plant vacuole called?
rationales: Correct: the membrane of a plant vacuole is called the tonoplast.
A crista is a fold of the inner membrane of a mitochondrion.
A centriole is an organelle involved in forming spindle fibres and basal bodies.
Cisternae are the flattened sacs that make up the Golgi apparatus.

options: Long and always present in pairs
mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly compares cilia and flagella?
rationales: Correct: cilia are short and usually numerous, while flagella are longer and fewer.
Flagella are longer but are usually fewer, not numerous.
Cilia are usually numerous, not few.
Flagella are longer and fewer; they are not always present in pairs.

written.text: What are the main functions of cell membrane?
written.finalAnswer: It forms a boundary around the cytoplasm and controls what substances enter and leave the cell.

rubric.why: The membrane’s boundary role is one of its main functions.
rubric.description: State that it forms a boundary around the cytoplasm.
rubric.how: Mention that the membrane surrounds the cytoplasm.

rubric.why: Control of substances entering and leaving is the key function asked for.
rubric.description: State that it controls what substances enter and leave the cell.
rubric.how: Name both entry and exit of substances.

modelAnswer: The cell membrane forms a boundary around the cytoplasm.
It controls what substances enter and leave the cell.

written.text: What key role does the Golgi apparatus play in eukaryotic cells?
written.finalAnswer: It modifies proteins coming from rough ER and packs them into Golgi vesicles for use in the cell or transport outside it.

rubric.why: Modification of proteins from rough ER is an important part of the Golgi apparatus’s role.
rubric.description: State that it modifies proteins coming from rough ER.
rubric.how: Name both the protein material and modification.

rubric.why: Packing proteins into vesicles is the other key role requested.
rubric.description: State that it packs the products into vesicles for use or secretion.
rubric.how: Mention vesicles and their destination or use.

modelAnswer: The Golgi apparatus modifies proteins coming from rough ER.
It packs them into Golgi vesicles for use in the cell or transport outside it.

written.text: How do lysosomes contribute to the cell's functioning?
written.finalAnswer: Lysosomes digest food, break down cellular wastes and damaged organelles, and can store certain molecules for later use.

rubric.why: Digestion of food material is a function described for lysosomes.
rubric.description: Explain that lysosomal enzymes digest food in food vacuoles.
rubric.how: Mention food digestion.

rubric.why: Breakdown of wastes or damaged organelles is another important contribution.
rubric.description: State that lysosomes break down cellular wastes or damaged organelles.
rubric.how: Name at least one of these materials.

modelAnswer: Lysosomes fuse with food vacuoles and their digestive enzymes break down the food.
They also break down cellular wastes and damaged organelles.
They can store certain molecules for later use.

written.text: What is the smooth endoplasmic reticulum responsible for?
written.finalAnswer: It is involved in lipid metabolism, transport of materials through the cell, and detoxification of harmful chemicals; in muscle cells it also helps in contraction.

rubric.why: Lipid metabolism is a stated function of smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
rubric.description: Name its role in lipid metabolism.
rubric.how: Use the term lipid or lipid metabolism.

rubric.why: Transport or detoxification identifies an additional function of SER.
rubric.description: Name transport of materials or detoxification of harmful chemicals.
rubric.how: State at least one additional function.

modelAnswer: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum is involved in lipid metabolism.
It transports materials from one part of the cell to another and detoxifies harmful chemicals.
In muscle cells, it is also involved in contraction.

written.text: How do the vacuoles in plant cells differ from vacuoles in animal cells?
written.finalAnswer: Most mature plant cells have one large central vacuole containing cell sap, while animal cells may have many small temporary vacuoles containing water and food substances.

rubric.why: The large central vacuole is the key plant-cell feature in the comparison.
rubric.description: Describe the usual plant-cell vacuole.
rubric.how: State that it is usually one large central vacuole in mature plant cells.

rubric.why: The animal-cell arrangement completes the comparison.
rubric.description: Describe animal-cell vacuoles and their contents.
rubric.how: Mention that animal cells may have many small temporary vacuoles.

modelAnswer: Most mature plant cells have one large central vacuole containing cell sap.
Animal cells may have many small temporary vacuoles containing water and food substances.

written.text: Why are the cristae important for cellular respiration?
written.finalAnswer: Cristae increase the surface area for respiration in mitochondria.

rubric.why: Cristae are folds of the mitochondrial inner membrane.
rubric.description: Identify the cristae as folds of the inner membrane.
rubric.how: Refer to the inner mitochondrial membrane.

rubric.why: The increased surface area explains their importance for respiration.
rubric.description: Explain that they increase surface area for respiration.
rubric.how: Link increased surface area to respiration.

modelAnswer: Cristae are folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
They increase the surface area for respiration.

written.text: How are chromatin and chromosomes related?
written.finalAnswer: Chromatin is made of DNA and proteins. When a cell starts dividing, chromatin condenses and takes the shape of thick chromosomes.

rubric.why: This identifies what chromatin is made of.
rubric.description: State that chromatin consists of DNA and proteins.
rubric.how: Name both DNA and proteins.

rubric.why: The change from chromatin to chromosomes directly answers the relationship.
rubric.description: Explain that chromatin condenses into chromosomes when the cell starts dividing.
rubric.how: Include condensation and chromosome formation.

modelAnswer: Chromatin is made of DNA and proteins.
When a cell starts dividing, chromatin condenses and takes the shape of thick chromosomes.

written.text:
Name the chemical compounds that make up:
(a) Cell membrane
(b) Fungal cell wall
(c) Plant cell wall
(d) Bacterial cell wall
(e) Ribosomes
(f) Chromosomes
written.finalAnswer:
(a) Proteins, lipids and small quantities of carbohydrates
(b) Chitin
(c) Cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin in the primary wall; cellulose, lignin and other chemicals in the secondary wall
(d) Peptidoglycan
(e) Proteins and ribosomal RNA (rRNA)
(f) DNA and proteins

rubric.why: These are the stated components of the cell membrane.
rubric.description: Give the compounds in the cell membrane.
rubric.how: Name proteins and lipids, and include small quantities of carbohydrates for full accuracy.

rubric.why: Chitin is the defining wall material stated for fungi.
rubric.description: Name the fungal cell-wall material.
rubric.how: Write chitin.

rubric.why: The plant-wall composition is a key part of the multi-part question.
rubric.description: Give the stated plant cell-wall materials.
rubric.how: Include primary-wall materials and, where relevant, secondary-wall materials.

rubric.why: Peptidoglycan identifies the bacterial cell-wall material.
rubric.description: Name the bacterial cell-wall material.
rubric.how: Write peptidoglycan.

rubric.why: The answer must also identify ribosome and chromosome composition.
rubric.description: Give the stated compositions of ribosomes and chromosomes.
rubric.how: State that ribosomes contain proteins and rRNA and chromosomes contain DNA and proteins.

modelAnswer: (a) Cell membrane: proteins, lipids and small quantities of carbohydrates.
(b) Fungal cell wall: chitin.
(c) Plant cell wall: the primary wall is mainly cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; the secondary wall is mainly cellulose, lignin and other chemicals.
(d) Bacterial cell wall: peptidoglycan.
(e) Ribosomes: almost equal amounts of proteins and ribosomal RNA (rRNA).
(f) Chromosomes: DNA and proteins.

written.text: Explain the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane.
written.finalAnswer: The cell membrane has a fluid-like lipid bilayer with protein molecules submerged in it. Lipids and proteins move laterally, so their mosaic pattern constantly changes. Carbohydrates join proteins as glycoproteins or lipids as glycolipids.

rubric.why: The lipid bilayer is the foundation of the model.
rubric.description: Describe the fluid-like lipid bilayer.
rubric.how: State that lipids form a bilayer.

rubric.why: The proteins’ position in the bilayer is central to the model.
rubric.description: Explain that proteins are submerged in the bilayer.
rubric.how: Place protein molecules within the lipid bilayer.

rubric.why: Lateral movement explains why the membrane is called fluid.
rubric.description: State that lipids and proteins can move laterally.
rubric.how: Mention movement within the membrane.

rubric.why: Carbohydrate attachments complete the textbook description of the model.
rubric.description: Describe carbohydrate attachment to proteins or lipids.
rubric.how: Name glycoproteins and glycolipids, or explain both attachments.

modelAnswer: The cell membrane is composed of proteins, lipids and small quantities of carbohydrates.
According to the fluid-mosaic model, the lipids make a fluid-like bilayer in which protein molecules are submerged.
The lipids and proteins can move laterally, so the mosaic pattern constantly changes.
Carbohydrates join proteins as glycoproteins or lipids as glycolipids.

written.text: Describe the structure and functions of the cell wall.
written.finalAnswer: The cell wall is a rigid, non-living wall around the cell membrane. It provides shape, strength, protection and support to the protoplasm. The plant cell wall has a middle lamella, primary wall and secondary wall; plasmodesmata allow molecules to pass between adjacent cells.

rubric.why: A correct description begins with the wall’s nature and position.
rubric.description: Describe the cell wall as rigid, non-living and around the cell membrane.
rubric.how: Include its non-living nature and location.

rubric.why: Its functions are an essential part of the question.
rubric.description: Give the wall’s support and protective functions.
rubric.how: Name at least two of its stated functions.

rubric.why: The plant cell wall’s layers show its structure.
rubric.description: Name the three plant cell-wall layers.
rubric.how: List middle lamella, primary wall and secondary wall.

rubric.why: The composition of its layers adds important structural detail.
rubric.description: Give the main materials in the plant cell-wall layers.
rubric.how: Name primary-wall materials and/or secondary-wall materials.

rubric.why: Plasmodesmata explain how adjacent cells exchange molecules through their walls.
rubric.description: Explain the function of plasmodesmata.
rubric.how: State that these channels allow exchange between adjacent cells.

modelAnswer: The cell wall is a rigid, non-living wall around the cell membrane.
It provides shape, strength, protection and support to the protoplasm.
The plant cell wall has three layers: middle lamella, primary wall and secondary wall.
The primary wall is mainly made of cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin; the secondary wall is mainly made of cellulose, lignin and other chemicals.
Plasmodesmata are channels in cell walls that allow the exchange of molecules between adjacent cells.

written.text: Discuss the components of the nucleus.
written.finalAnswer: The nucleus is bounded by a semi-permeable double nuclear envelope with pores. Its nucleoplasm contains nucleoli, where ribosomes are assembled, and chromatin made of DNA and proteins. Chromatin condenses into chromosomes when the cell divides. DNA contains genes that control cell activities and transmit characteristics.

rubric.why: The nuclear envelope and pores describe the nucleus’s boundary.
rubric.description: Describe the nuclear envelope and its pores.
rubric.how: State that it is a double membrane with pores.

rubric.why: Nucleoplasm is an important internal component.
rubric.description: Name the nucleoplasm inside the nucleus.
rubric.how: Identify it as the inner jelly-like material.

rubric.why: The nucleoli and their function are another key component.
rubric.description: Name the nucleoli and explain their role.
rubric.how: State that ribosomes are assembled there.

rubric.why: Chromatin and DNA explain the genetic role of the nucleus.
rubric.description: Describe chromatin and DNA’s role.
rubric.how: Mention DNA and proteins, chromosome formation, or DNA’s genes and control.

modelAnswer: The nucleus is bounded by a double membrane called the nuclear envelope, which has many nuclear pores.
The inner jelly-like material is called nucleoplasm.
The nucleoplasm contains one or more nucleoli, where ribosomes are assembled.
It also contains chromatin, made of DNA and proteins; chromatin condenses into thick chromosomes when a cell starts dividing.
DNA contains genes that control cell activities and transmits characteristics to the next generation.

written.text: Describe the structure and function of lysosome and endoplasmic reticulum.
written.finalAnswer: Lysosomes are small membrane-bound vesicles containing digestive enzymes; they digest food and break down cellular wastes and damaged organelles. The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of membrane-bounded channels in eukaryotic cells. Rough ER has ribosomes and functions in protein synthesis. Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is involved in lipid metabolism, transport and detoxification.

rubric.why: This describes the structure and contents of lysosomes.
rubric.description: Describe lysosome structure.
rubric.how: Mention membrane-bound vesicles containing digestive enzymes.

rubric.why: Lysosome functions are a required part of the answer.
rubric.description: Give the digestive and breakdown functions of lysosomes.
rubric.how: Mention food, wastes or damaged organelles.

rubric.why: This identifies the overall structure of endoplasmic reticulum.
rubric.description: Describe the endoplasmic reticulum as a channel network.
rubric.how: State that it is a network of membrane-bounded channels in eukaryotic cells.

rubric.why: The rough ER’s ribosomes and protein function distinguish it from SER.
rubric.description: Describe the rough ER and its function.
rubric.how: Link attached ribosomes to protein synthesis.

rubric.why: The smooth ER has its own distinct functions to describe.
rubric.description: Describe smooth ER functions.
rubric.how: Mention lipid metabolism, transport or detoxification.

modelAnswer: Lysosomes are small membrane-bound vesicles that contain digestive enzymes.
They digest food in food vacuoles and break down cellular wastes and damaged organelles.
The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of membrane-bounded channels throughout the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells.
Rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes attached to its surface and functions in protein synthesis.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes; it is involved in lipid metabolism, transport of materials and detoxification of harmful chemicals.

written.text: Describe the structure and functions of the chloroplast.
written.finalAnswer: Chloroplasts are double-membrane-bound green plastids containing chlorophyll. Their thylakoids are stacked into grana and surrounded by stroma. They contain DNA and ribosomes. Chloroplasts capture light energy and use it to prepare glucose by photosynthesis.

rubric.why: This identifies the chloroplast and its enclosing membranes.
rubric.description: Describe chloroplasts as green plastids enclosed by a double membrane.
rubric.how: Mention their green colour or double membrane.

rubric.why: The internal membrane arrangement is a key structural feature.
rubric.description: Describe thylakoids and grana.
rubric.how: Explain that thylakoids are sac-like structures stacked into grana.

rubric.why: These details complete the chloroplast’s internal structure.
rubric.description: Name the stroma and/or its DNA and ribosomes.
rubric.how: Identify the fluid stroma and include its own DNA and ribosomes.

rubric.why: Pigments on thylakoids capture light energy.
rubric.description: State that chlorophyll or photosynthetic pigments are present.
rubric.how: Link the pigment to capturing light.

rubric.why: Photosynthesis and glucose production give the chloroplast’s main function.
rubric.description: Explain its role in photosynthesis and glucose preparation.
rubric.how: State that captured light energy is used to prepare glucose.

modelAnswer: Chloroplasts are green plastids present in green parts of plants and in algae; they are enclosed by a double membrane.
Inside, sets of stacked membranes called grana are present; each granum is made of sac-like thylakoids.
Photosynthetic pigments such as chlorophyll are present on the surface of thylakoids, and stroma surrounds them.
Chloroplasts contain their own DNA and ribosomes.
They capture light energy and convert it into chemical energy, which they use to prepare glucose by photosynthesis.

written.text: What impact might mitochondrial dysfunction or absence have on other organelles' ability to operate in a cell?
written.finalAnswer: Mitochondrial dysfunction or absence would reduce the cell’s ATP supply from aerobic respiration. With less energy, energy-requiring processes in other organelles, such as protein production, transport and cell maintenance, could slow down or fail.

rubric.why: The answer needs to connect mitochondria to the cell’s energy supply.
rubric.description: State that mitochondria produce energy through aerobic respiration.
rubric.how: Mention energy or ATP production and respiration.

rubric.why: Reduced ATP is the immediate effect of mitochondrial dysfunction or absence.
rubric.description: Explain that the cell would have less ATP or energy.
rubric.how: State the expected reduction in energy supply.

rubric.why: The question asks how other organelles would be affected.
rubric.description: Explain that energy-dependent organelle processes could slow or fail.
rubric.how: Link reduced energy to the operation of other organelles.

rubric.why: An example makes the impact specific and reasoned.
rubric.description: Give an example of an affected process.
rubric.how: Name protein production, transport or cell maintenance.

modelAnswer: Mitochondria produce energy in the form of ATP during aerobic respiration.
If mitochondria are dysfunctional or absent, the cell’s ATP supply would be reduced.
Energy-requiring processes in other organelles, such as protein production, transport and cell maintenance, could slow down or fail.
Therefore, the normal functioning of the cell would be affected.

examTips: Short questions often ask for an organelle’s function, composition or comparison; give the key term and a precise function.
Long questions commonly ask for structure and function together. Organise the answer by naming the structure, describing its parts, then explaining what it does.
For the fluid-mosaic model, include the lipid bilayer, submerged proteins, lateral movement and carbohydrate attachments.
For comparisons, write both sides clearly. For example, contrast the large central plant vacuole with the small temporary animal vacuoles.
Marks are earned for correct textbook terms and complete points; do not replace a specific function with a vague statement such as “it helps the cell.”

steps.why: Start with the membrane’s basic arrangement in the fluid-mosaic model.
steps.text: The lipids make a fluid-like bilayer.

steps.why: The proteins are part of the mosaic and lie within the lipid bilayer.
steps.text: Protein molecules are submerged in the bilayer.

steps.why: Movement of these molecules makes the membrane fluid and its pattern changeable.
steps.text: The lipids and proteins can move laterally, so the mosaic pattern constantly changes.

steps.why: Carbohydrate attachments are another feature of the model.

example.question: Describe the fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane.
example.answer: The lipids make a fluid-like bilayer in which proteins are submerged. Lipids and proteins move laterally, so the mosaic pattern constantly changes. Carbohydrates join proteins as glycoproteins or lipids as glycolipids.

explain.title: Cell wall
explain.body: The cells of bacteria, fungi, plants and some protists (algae) have a rigid non-living wall around cell membrane. It is called cell wall. It provides shape, strength, protection and support to the inner living matter (protoplasm) of the cell. Plant walls have a middle lamella, primary wall and secondary wall. Plasmodesmata are channels that allow molecule exchange between adjacent cells.

explain.title: Cell membrane
explain.body: All cells have a thin and elastic cell membrane around the cytoplasm. It is selectively-permeable. It allows very few molecules to pass through it while blocks many other molecules. Its fluid-mosaic model has a fluid-like lipid bilayer with proteins submerged in it; lipids and proteins can move laterally.

explain.title: Cytoplasm and nucleus
explain.body: It is the jelly-like substance that fills the inside of a cell. Cytoplasm provides a medium for organelles to move and function and is a site for metabolic reactions. The nucleus is the cell’s control center; its DNA contains genes that control cell activities and transmit characteristics.

explain.title: Cell structures that make and move materials
explain.body: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis. Rough ER has ribosomes and functions in protein synthesis; smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is involved in lipid metabolism, transport and detoxification. The Golgi apparatus modifies proteins and packs them into vesicles.

explain.title: Energy, storage and movement
explain.body: Mitochondria produce ATP during aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts capture light energy and use it to prepare glucose. Vacuoles store fluid and other materials; the large central vacuole in mature plant cells helps keep them turgid. Cilia and flagella function in movement.

mistakes: Do not say that the cell wall is living; the textbook describes it as rigid and non-living.
Do not confuse the primary wall, secondary wall and middle lamella or their positions.
Do not describe the cell membrane as fully permeable; it is selectively-permeable.
Do not say that nucleoli control the cell: ribosomes are assembled there, while the nucleus directs cellular activities.
Do not confuse rough ER with smooth ER: rough ER has ribosomes; smooth ER lacks them.
Do not confuse mitochondrial cristae with chloroplast grana or thylakoids.
When comparing plant and animal vacuoles, include both the large central plant vacuole and the small temporary animal vacuoles.
